I don't see much of a point of this method of space launch since it looks like by around 2020 there will be rocket-jet hybrid engines, i.e. the SABRE by Reaction Engines. This stratolaunch vehicle basically separates out the rocket and the jet part, while the SABRE combines them, which reduces part count, complexity, weight, and so cost.

However, there is always the tiny possibility that the SABRE guys developing that method fail, and so the Stratolaunch guys act as a kind of unlikely-to-be-needed back up.

But still, this method has been tried before, and it doesn't end up much, if any, cheaper than just piggybacking a ride with a larger satellite launch on a conventional rocket.

IMHO, I think these guys are about 30-40 years behind with this one.

EDIT1: Some extra info...In terms of this being tried before, an example is the Pegasus rocket. It never really worked (okay, it's done a few launches, but compare it to some of the more mainstream rockets and you'll see why these rocket-attached-to-plane methods are so uncommon) because it had a very low reliability when it comes to what is wanted for spacecraft, and it never ended up being cheaper than piggybacking. I know that advances in technology could make the method plausible (more cheaper than piggybacking), but meh, there are a lot of better methods that are being developed that look likely to be much cheaper.

I mean there's SpaceX and their reusable method. That would instantly invalidate the stratolauncher on cost. And as previously said, the SABRE method would also likely be cheaper. I'm not sure what numbers these guys are using that makes them think their stratolauncher will be cheaper, it's pretty crazy...

Why build the largest plane in the world to put a satellite into space? A setup like the Stratolaunch can allow flexible satellite launches during a range of weather conditions and from anywhere in the world…with a runway big enough, that is. Those are two things a stationary launch pad can’t do.

You are right that weather-flexibilities of the Stratolauncher is better than SpaceX could ever achieve with their future reusable rocket solutions...

But then the SKYLON which Reaction Engines are working on is basically the Stratolauncher but better. The jet-aircraft and the rocket are as one, and I can't see any cons of that concept. As explained in the original comment, it reduces part count and so complexity, probably increases reliability therefore, and costs less.
